children: Chief Executive Sergio Ermotti is urging Swiss lawmakers to soften proposed capital requirements ahead of a parliamentary vote that could significantly raise the bank’s operating costs.
Switzerland’s upper house is scheduled to vote Wednesday on regulations designed to reduce the risk of another banking crisis. The measures were proposed after UBS
acquired Credit Suisse in a government-backed rescue in 2023.
The government’s plan could require UBS

to hold about $20 billion in additional capital. A central provision would force the bank to support its foreign subsidiaries entirely with Common Equity Tier 1 capital, the most expensive and loss-absorbing form of bank funding.
Ermotti told the Neue Zürcher Zeitung that UBS
accepts the need for stronger safeguards but considers the full requirement excessive. He argued that the added expense would eventually affect customers and employees, not just shareholders.

A parliamentary committee has proposed allowing UBS to meet half the requirement with Additional Tier 1 securities, a less costly form of capital. UBS estimates that approach would require it to raise about $13 billion in AT1 funding. Ermotti described the option as difficult but manageable.

Some lawmakers have instead expressed support for requiring 90% of the foreign-subsidiary exposure to be backed by CET1 capital. Ermotti said that proposal would still place an unreasonable burden on the bank.

For investors, the final rules could influence UBS’s profitability, capital returns and valuation. A heavier reliance on CET1 capital could constrain share buybacks and dividends while raising the cost of operating from Switzerland. A compromise involving AT1 securities would likely reduce those pressures, though it would still increase funding costs.
UBS Chairman Colm Kelleher previously warned that the bank may reconsider its long-term position in Switzerland if the regulations leave it unable to compete internationally.

title: UBS CEO pushes back on Swiss capital rules ahead of parliamentary vote
